evening.title: Made in India vs Made in France Rafale: Breaking Down the True Cost of the MRFA Deal
evening.text:
As India moves closer to issuing the Request for Proposal (RFP) for its 114-aircraft Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft (MRFA) programme, one question continues to surface: Would a Rafale manufactured in India actually be cheaper than one built in France?
The answer is more nuanced than a simple comparison of price tags. If only the factory cost of producing each aircraft is considered, a Rafale assembled in India is unlikely to be cheaper during the initial production phase. However, when the aircraft’s entire operational life—spanning three to four decades—is taken into account, local production could generate substantial savings while significantly strengthening India’s aerospace ecosystem.
Understanding the distinction between flyaway cost and lifecycle cost is essential.
The flyaway cost refers to the price of the aircraft itself, including its airframe, engines, avionics and factory testing. It excludes weapons, simulators, infrastructure, training, maintenance support and long-term logistics.
French budget documents and previous procurement data indicate that the flyaway cost of a standard French Air and Space Force Rafale generally falls in the range of approximately US$85–105 million, depending on configuration and production batch. Export contracts often appear much higher because they include weapons, training, maintenance packages, infrastructure and performance-based logistics.
If India establishes a domestic Rafale production line under the MRFA programme, industry analysts generally expect the early aircraft produced in India to cost more on a flyaway basis than aircraft rolling directly off Dassault Aviation’s established production line in France. The precise premium would depend on the final level of localisation, production volume and technology transfer arrangements, but initial locally manufactured aircraft typically carry higher unit costs until production matures.
This pattern is not unique to India.
Licensed fighter production has historically involved a learning curve during which manufacturing efficiency gradually improves as local industry gains experience. Countries including South Korea, Japan and even India itself experienced similar cost premiums during the initial phases of licensed military aircraft production.
The largest contributor to higher early costs is the establishment of manufacturing infrastructure.
Producing a fourth-and-a-half-generation fighter requires sophisticated tooling, precision machining centres, composite manufacturing facilities, automated drilling systems, quality assurance laboratories and highly specialised testing equipment. Building this industrial ecosystem involves substantial capital investment that must be recovered over the production run.
If India manufactures around 90–100 aircraft locally, these fixed investments are spread across a relatively limited number of airframes, increasing the effective cost of each aircraft during the programme’s initial years.
Technology transfer also carries significant costs.
Unlike importing completed aircraft, licensed production requires transferring manufacturing processes, specialised tooling, engineering documentation, quality standards and workforce training. These investments create long-term industrial capability but inevitably increase programme costs in the early stages.
India is also expected to seek substantial customisation beyond the standard French configuration.
The Indian Air Force’s current Rafale fleet already incorporates several India-Specific Enhancements (ISE), including customised communication systems, electronic warfare improvements and operational modifications tailored to Indian requirements.
Future MRFA aircraft could potentially incorporate additional indigenous technologies over time, including compatibility with the Astra family of beyond-visual-range missiles, future indigenous precision-guided weapons and other Indian-developed subsystems. Any such integration would require engineering, software validation, flight testing and certification, adding further costs beyond those associated with a standard production aircraft.
Another factor limiting immediate cost reductions is localisation itself.
Even if India achieves significant indigenous content, several highly specialised components are likely to continue being sourced from France, particularly during the early years of production. These may include engine core technologies, certain avionics modules, specialised sensors and proprietary software elements that remain under the control of the original manufacturer.
Consequently, local assembly does not eliminate dependence on imported high-value components.
However, the economic picture changes dramatically once the aircraft enters long-term service.
Modern fighter aircraft typically remain operational for 35 to 40 years, during which acquisition costs represent only part of total expenditure. Maintenance, repairs, upgrades, spare parts, depot overhauls and lifecycle support often exceed the original purchase price over the aircraft’s lifetime.
This is where domestic production offers its greatest financial advantage.
A local manufacturing ecosystem enables India to establish indigenous Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facilities capable of supporting the fleet without relying extensively on overseas repair chains. Aircraft spend less time awaiting imported components, transportation costs decline and depot-level maintenance can be performed domestically.
Local production also encourages the development of Indian suppliers capable of manufacturing components, structural assemblies and consumables. As indigenous content expands, dependence on imported spares gradually decreases, insulating the fleet from currency fluctuations, overseas production bottlenecks and geopolitical disruptions.
Operational availability also improves.
Faster access to replacement parts and domestic repair facilities allows more aircraft to remain mission-ready at any given time—an important consideration for an air force managing large operational commitments across two active frontiers.
There are broader strategic benefits as well.
A domestic Rafale production line would develop advanced aerospace manufacturing skills, expand India’s precision engineering capabilities and strengthen local supply chains. These capabilities could support future indigenous programmes, including the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), as well as civil aerospace manufacturing.
Technology transfer in areas such as composites, precision machining, avionics integration and systems engineering would have long-term value extending well beyond the MRFA programme itself.
The experience gained could also improve India’s ability to independently undertake future upgrades without relying exclusively on overseas engineering support.
From Dassault Aviation’s perspective, local production may also prove commercially attractive by securing one of the world’s largest fighter aircraft orders while establishing an enduring industrial partnership in India.
Ultimately, comparing a French-built Rafale with a locally manufactured aircraft depends on which metric is used.
If only the initial manufacturing cost is considered, aircraft produced in France are likely to remain less expensive because their production infrastructure has already been amortised over hundreds of aircraft built during the past two decades.
However, if the analysis extends across the aircraft’s entire service life, local production begins to shift the balance. Reduced maintenance costs, faster logistics, domestic repair capability, improved fleet availability and industrial self-reliance can offset much of the higher acquisition cost while delivering strategic benefits that cannot be measured purely in dollars.

evening.title: Why India’s Army Should Build a Multi-Layer Drone Wall for Future Warfare
evening.text:
Future wars are unlikely to be decided by static defensive positions alone. Instead, they will be shaped by layered networks of unmanned systems that can detect, track, jam and destroy enemy formations long before they reach the contact line. As the Indian Army transitions toward Integrated Battle Groups (IBGs), one concept that deserves serious attention is the creation of a 40-km-deep unmanned kill web combining intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), loitering munitions, FPV drones, electronic warfare and counter-drone systems.
Rather than viewing the battlefield as a single front line, the concept divides it into multiple engagement belts extending from the contact line to roughly 40 kilometres into enemy-held territory. Every layer performs a specific function, ensuring attackers are continuously detected, disrupted and attrited before launching an assault.
The outermost layer would focus on persistent ISR. Long-endurance drones equipped with electro-optical, infrared and synthetic aperture radar payloads could monitor enemy assembly areas, logistics nodes and artillery positions. This intelligence would feed directly into command networks, allowing IBGs to identify concentrations of armour, mechanised infantry and missile launchers well before they begin offensive operations.
Once hostile forces are detected, the next layer would consist of long-range loitering munitions and precision artillery. Rather than waiting for enemy formations to approach Indian positions, autonomous strike systems could engage artillery batteries, command vehicles, air-defence radars and ammunition depots deep behind the front. Destroying these high-value targets early would significantly reduce the combat power available to an advancing force.
As enemy columns move closer, the emphasis would shift toward disrupting logistics. FPV drones, autonomous strike UAVs and precision-guided munitions could target fuel tankers, engineering vehicles, bridge-laying equipment and supply convoys. Modern mechanised formations depend heavily on uninterrupted logistics, and sustained drone attacks against these assets could slow or even halt an offensive without engaging frontline combat units directly.
The final defensive belts would become increasingly dense with short-range FPV drones, loitering munitions and anti-armour systems. Swarms of inexpensive FPV drones could engage tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and assault engineers attempting to breach defensive positions. Because FPV drones are relatively low-cost compared to tanks or armoured vehicles, they offer defenders an economically favourable way to impose heavy losses on attacking forces.
Equally important would be the integration of counter-unmanned aerial systems (C-UAS). Every layer of the kill web would require electronic warfare systems capable of detecting, jamming or neutralising hostile drones. Mobile anti-drone radars, radio-frequency jammers, directed-energy weapons and interceptor drones could create protected corridors for Indian forces while denying similar advantages to the adversary.
Artificial intelligence would serve as the backbone of this architecture. Thousands of sensors, drones and ground systems would continuously generate enormous volumes of battlefield data. AI-enabled command systems could automatically prioritise targets, allocate weapons, coordinate drone swarms and recommend engagement sequences within seconds, significantly compressing the sensor-to-shooter cycle.
Such a layered defence would also complement India’s ongoing investments in indigenous drone technologies. Systems developed by DRDO and Indian private industry—including ISR UAVs, loitering munitions, autonomous logistics drones and electronic warfare platforms—could all contribute to different layers of the kill web. Combined with satellite imagery, battlefield communication networks and integrated fire-control systems, these assets would enable IBGs to operate as highly networked combat formations.
The objective is not merely to stop an enemy at the front line but to degrade combat power continuously across depth. By the time hostile forces reach Indian defensive positions, they would ideally have already suffered losses in reconnaissance assets, logistics, artillery, command networks and armoured spearheads.
evening.summary: Future wars are unlikely to be decided by static defensive positions alone. Instead, they will be shaped by layered networks of unmanned systems that can detect, track, jam and destroy enemy formation

evening.title: “Is India Now in Europe?”: German Analysts React as New Delhi Eyes France-Led Sixth-Generation Fighter Programme
evening.text:
India’s reported move to explore participation in a French-led sixth-generation fighter programme has triggered a sharp reaction across European defence circles, with some German commentators questioning what India’s involvement could mean for Europe’s own next-generation combat-aircraft ambitions. The debate has quickly spilled onto social media, with supporters and critics trading increasingly provocative assessments of whether India could become a partner in Europe’s future fighter ecosystem.
The immediate trigger is a statement presented to India’s Parliamentary Standing Committee on Defence. According to the Defence Ministry, India has formally initiated efforts to join a sixth-generation fighter development programme spearheaded by the French government. The development was first reported by Indian media and represents a significant change in India’s long-term combat-aircraft planning.
The wording is important. India has initiated efforts; that does not mean New Delhi has joined the programme, secured an invitation from France, or obtained a formal development role. Nevertheless, the announcement is significant because it comes after the breakdown of the Franco-German industrial relationship surrounding FCAS and as India’s own AMCA programme moves forward.
The resulting social-media debate has produced a provocative question: “Is India now in Europe, or is France now arming in an un-European way?”
The question is rhetorical, but it captures the underlying industrial and strategic dilemma. France has traditionally insisted on strategic autonomy and sovereign control over critical military technologies. India, meanwhile, has increasingly sought access to advanced technologies through co-development rather than simply purchasing finished foreign equipment.
Some German defence commentators have reacted sceptically. One argument circulating online is that anyone assuming India would be an easier development partner than Germany has “got it dead wrong”, with another commentator warning that those who thought cooperation with Germany was difficult were about to discover a “whole new meaning” of difficulty.
These comments should be treated as commentary rather than established assessments. There is no evidence that Germany, France or India has formally assessed the other country in these terms. The remarks nevertheless expose the deeper problem that destroyed the original FCAS arrangement: sixth-generation combat aircraft are not merely weapons programmes; they are enormous industrial and technological partnerships involving workshare, intellectual property, design authority, export policy and national sovereignty.
France’s position is particularly distinctive. Paris has long placed a premium on independent control over its nuclear deterrent, combat-aircraft design and weapons systems. France is therefore unlikely to accept an international partnership in which its ability to determine the evolution of the future fighter becomes subordinate to another participant.
India could actually find this model attractive.
New Delhi has repeatedly sought technology sovereignty, domestic manufacturing and freedom to modify imported systems. Its interest in a future French programme would therefore potentially be less about buying a French sixth-generation aircraft and more about gaining a defined role in the development of advanced propulsion, sensors, electronic warfare, autonomous systems, mission computing and combat-cloud technologies.
That is where the German reaction becomes interesting.
The original FCAS experience demonstrated that industrial cooperation between technologically advanced countries can become extremely complicated when the partners cannot agree on who controls the core fighter. The breakdown between Dassault Aviation and Airbus was widely associated with disagreements over industrial leadership and workshare. Recent European commentary has described the collapse as a major setback for European strategic autonomy.
Adding India would introduce another major industrial player, but it would also potentially provide France with something it has increasingly valued: a partner outside the traditional European industrial structure.
For India, however, there is an equally important warning. New Delhi should not enter a French sixth-generation programme merely to become another customer or manufacturing subcontractor. If India participates, it would need meaningful design and technology responsibilities, particularly in areas that complement the indigenous AMCA programme.
The two programmes could theoretically be complementary. AMCA would provide India with its own fifth-generation combat-aircraft design and an indigenous pathway toward advanced fighter development. Participation in a French sixth-generation programme could expose Indian engineers to technologies that India may otherwise take decades to develop independently.
France could also benefit from Indian participation. India’s expanding aerospace manufacturing sector, large engineering workforce and growing defence market could provide additional industrial capacity and a potential long-term customer base.
But the social-media war is also revealing something else: India’s strategic importance is no longer being discussed only as a buyer of European weapons. It is increasingly being discussed as a potential participant in the design of Europe’s future combat systems.
That does not mean India is “in Europe.” Nor does it mean France has abandoned European defence cooperation. It means Paris and New Delhi may increasingly see value in building defence-industrial relationships that extend beyond traditional European structures.

evening.title: Why the AMCA Mk2’s 2036 Deadline Hinges on Signing the 120kN Engine JV by End-2026
evening.text:
If India is serious about getting the AMCA Mk2 into service by 2036, the clock on choosing a foreign partner for its indigenous 120kN-class fighter engine is running out fast. Rolls-Royce’s own final proposal makes this timeline explicit, and it leaves essentially no room for the decision to slip past the end of this year.
Rolls-Royce Has Put a Hard Date on the Table
Rolls-Royce’s final proposal for the AMCA’s 120kN engine states that if an agreement is finalised by the end of 2026, testing of the engine’s core components could begin by 2030, paving the way for the engine’s maiden flight in 2034 and full-scale production by 2036. Sashi Mukundan, Rolls-Royce’s executive vice president for India, has publicly positioned the company as one of only three genuine aero-engine manufacturers in the world, alongside two American firms — implicitly setting up Rolls-Royce against Safran, the other finalist for this contract.
Under the AMCA’s phased plan, the initial batch of aircraft will fly on the GE F414 engine — the same powerplant selected for the Tejas Mk2 — while the indigenous 120kN-class engine is reserved for later AMCA variants under Phase 2, with production originally targeted for 2035-36. That target production window is precisely why Rolls-Royce anchored its offer to an end-2026 signing deadline: miss it, and every subsequent milestone in the chain — core testing, first flight, full production — shifts to the right in lockstep.
Why GE’s Cost Escalation Forced This Reckoning
Both the Tejas Mk1A and Tejas Mk2 programmes are now contingent on American GE engines, and the AMCA Mk1 was heading in the same direction before a cost surge with GE forced a broader reassessment of India’s engine strategy. With GE’s costs rising and delivery delays mounting, the government now faces the question of whether to drop the GE engine altogether for the Mk2 and AMCA programmes — a decision that, if made, would force an accelerated selection of the foreign partner and an immediate start to indigenous engine development.
This cost dilemma is precisely why the Safran-versus-Rolls-Royce contest has taken on such urgency. Safran has offered 100 percent technology transfer, including full intellectual property rights and no export restrictions, building on its existing relationship with the IAF through the M88 engines that power India’s Rafale fleet, in collaboration with DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment in Bengaluru. Rolls-Royce has matched that offer of full technology transfer and complete IP ownership.
The Money on the Table Is Substantial
Both Safran and Rolls-Royce have submitted cost estimates for the 120kN engine project that could exceed $5 billion, making it one of the most expensive and critical indigenous aviation programmes in Indian history. In one reported development, a joint venture between GTRE and Safran was reportedly established at the end of 2025 to co-develop the 120kN engine, anchored to an announced commitment of $7 billion, with a longer-term trajectory toward a 140kN variant for a future 35-tonne stealth fighter design.
This scale of investment underscores why neither the government nor either bidder is treating the decision lightly — but it also means the negotiation itself, covering technology transfer terms, IP ownership, cost-sharing, and industrial workshare, is inherently complex and could easily consume months if not finalised with urgency.
What Happens If the Deadline Slips
The mechanics of Rolls-Royce’s own timeline reveal exactly how unforgiving this schedule is. Core testing by 2030 assumes work begins almost immediately after signing; a maiden flight by 2034 assumes core testing wraps on schedule; and full production by 2036 assumes the maiden flight itself doesn’t slip. Each stage in fighter engine development is sequential and highly interdependent — pushing the contract signature into 2027 doesn’t just delay the programme by a few months, it risks cascading delays across a decade-long development chain where fighter engine programmes worldwide have historically run over schedule even under ideal conditions.
This urgency is precisely what has driven the government to launch the National Aero Engine Mission in February 2026, aimed at coordinating India’s industry, academic institutions, and government laboratories toward long-term indigenous jet engine production — with Prime Minister Modi having set the direction on Independence Day 2025 by stating that India’s own fighter aircraft must have an Indian jet engine.
Parallel Indigenous Efforts Buy Some Cushion — But Not Much
India’s own Gas Turbine Research Establishment has separately been making progress on materials for a 120kN-class engine, with Hyderabad-based MIDHANI reported to have completed around 50 percent of the required alloys, with 80 percent of those already certified. GTRE is also advancing toward flight trials of an afterburning Kaveri-derived engine, potentially starting in the 73kN range and scaling upward, following a successful full afterburner test witnessed by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh in February 2026.
While encouraging, this indigenous work operates in a lower thrust class and on a slower maturation curve than what AMCA Mk2 requires — it strengthens India’s long-term negotiating position and technical base, but it isn’t a substitute for closing the JV deal on the timeline the 2036 target demands.
The Bottom Line
Every publicly available data point — Rolls-Royce’s own stated schedule, the sequential nature of engine core testing through first flight to production, and the government’s own urgency in launching the National Aero Engine Mission — points to the same conclusion: an end-2026 signing is not a nice-to-have, it’s the load-bearing assumption underneath the entire 2036 AMCA Mk2 service-entry target. Slip past this year without a signed JV, and 2036 stops being a real target and starts being an aspiration.

HAL Expands Unmanned Aviation Push with Rotary UAV Programme for High-Altitude Operations
evening.text:
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has confirmed that it is working on a Rotary Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (RUAV) designed to undertake logistics and Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions, particularly in India’s demanding high-altitude operational environment. The announcement reinforces HAL’s growing focus on autonomous aviation as militaries worldwide increasingly adopt unmanned systems to complement conventional aircraft. However, the company has not clarified whether the programme refers to the existing RUAV-200 developed jointly with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) or a larger unmanned version of the Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) Dhruv, concepts of which have previously been showcased by HAL.
The confirmation comes at a time when the Indian armed forces are placing greater emphasis on unmanned logistics platforms capable of sustaining troops deployed in difficult terrain while reducing the risks associated with manned helicopter operations. Rotary-wing UAVs are particularly valuable in mountainous regions because they can operate from confined spaces without requiring prepared runways and can transport essential supplies directly to remote forward posts.
HAL described the Rotary UAV as being intended for both logistics and ISR missions, highlighting its suitability for operations in challenging high-altitude conditions. Such dual-role capability would enable a single platform to transport supplies, monitor border areas, support disaster relief operations and provide persistent battlefield surveillance.
What remains unclear, however, is the exact platform HAL was referring to.
One possibility is the RUAV-200, an indigenous rotary-wing unmanned aerial vehicle jointly developed by HAL and DRDO. The aircraft has been specifically designed as a high-altitude logistics platform capable of autonomously transporting food, ammunition, medical supplies and other critical cargo to isolated military positions in mountainous regions. Often described as a “mule drone,” the RUAV-200 addresses one of the Indian Army’s longstanding operational challenges by reducing dependence on manned helicopter sorties for routine resupply missions in hazardous environments.
The RUAV-200 has already undergone developmental testing and represents one of India’s most mature rotary-wing unmanned logistics programmes. Its autonomous flight capability, vertical take-off and landing performance and ability to operate in difficult terrain make it well suited for supporting troops deployed along India’s northern borders.
The second possibility is considerably more ambitious. HAL has previously displayed conceptual designs for an unmanned version of the ALH Dhruv, transforming the proven utility helicopter into a larger autonomous platform capable of carrying heavier payloads over longer distances. Such a system would dramatically expand India’s unmanned logistics capability while also opening the possibility of conducting ISR, casualty evacuation, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions without exposing aircrew to hostile or hazardous conditions.
An unmanned Dhruv would offer significantly greater payload capacity and endurance than smaller rotary UAVs, enabling it to support a wider range of military operations. Its commonality with the existing Dhruv fleet could also simplify maintenance, logistics and manufacturing by leveraging HAL’s established production infrastructure and supply chain.
At present, HAL has not specified whether the Rotary UAV programme announced refers to further development of the RUAV-200, progression of the unmanned Dhruv concept or potentially both under a broader unmanned helicopter roadmap. Given the company’s expanding focus on autonomous systems, it is also possible that multiple rotary UAV programmes are being pursued simultaneously to address different operational requirements.
The announcement nevertheless reflects HAL’s strategic direction as unmanned aviation becomes an increasingly important component of future military operations. Around the world, armed forces are investing heavily in autonomous helicopters for logistics, surveillance, reconnaissance and battlefield support, recognising their ability to reduce operational risk while extending the reach of conventional forces.
For India, rotary UAVs could prove particularly valuable in the Himalayas, where difficult terrain, extreme weather and high-altitude conditions often complicate helicopter operations. Autonomous platforms capable of routinely delivering supplies, conducting surveillance or supporting military units would significantly enhance operational flexibility while freeing manned helicopters for more demanding combat and tactical missions.
evening.summary: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has confirmed that it is working on a Rotary Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (RUAV) designed to undertake logistics and Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR)

evening.title: Netra Mk2 vs Boeing E-7 Wedgetail: How India’s Indigenous AWACS Stacks Up Against the Global Benchmark
evening.text:
With the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Netra Mk2 Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) programme entering its execution phase, inevitable comparisons are being drawn with the Boeing E-7A Wedgetail, widely regarded as the global benchmark for modern narrow-body airborne early warning aircraft.
Although both aircraft are based on commercial single-aisle airliners and perform similar operational missions, they reflect two distinct engineering philosophies shaped by different operational requirements, industrial ecosystems and technological approaches.
Airframe: Airbus A321 vs Boeing 737
The Netra Mk2 is being developed on the Airbus A321, with six commercial aircraft undergoing conversion by AI Engineering Services Limited (AIESL) before mission-system integration by DRDO’s Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS) and Adani Defence Systems & Technologies Limited.
The A321 provides one of the largest cabins among single-aisle aircraft, offering greater internal volume than the Boeing 737 platform. This additional space allows for more operator consoles, expanded mission equipment, improved crew rest facilities and greater flexibility for future upgrades. The aircraft’s larger electrical power generation potential and payload capacity are also advantageous for carrying increasingly power-hungry radar and electronic warfare systems.
The Boeing E-7A Wedgetail, by comparison, is built on a modified Boeing 737 Next Generation platform, combining elements of the 737-700 fuselage with strengthened 737-800 wings. While physically smaller than the A321, the aircraft benefits from decades of operational maturity, extensive global logistics support and proven reliability.
The E-7 has already entered operational service with the Royal Australian Air Force, Turkish Air Force, Republic of Korea Air Force, and is being procured by the United States Air Force and Royal Air Force, giving it an unmatched operational pedigree among modern AEW&C aircraft.
Radar Architecture: Different Solutions to the Same Mission
The most significant distinction between the two aircraft lies in their radar architecture. The E-7A Wedgetail employs Northrop Grumman’s Multi-role Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) radar, mounted within its distinctive dorsal “Top Hat” antenna.
Unlike traditional rotating radars, the MESA system uses fixed Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) technology. Two large broadside arrays provide approximately 120 degrees of coverage each along the aircraft’s port and starboard sides, while additional end-fire arrays positioned at the front and rear of the antenna provide the remaining 60 degrees forward and aft. Together, these arrays deliver full 360-degree surveillance coverage without requiring any rotating mechanical structure.
Beyond airborne surveillance, the MESA radar also performs sophisticated Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) functions, enabling long-range detection and analysis of hostile radar emitters.
The Netra Mk2 adopts a different design philosophy.
Rather than relying on a single dorsal radar assembly for complete coverage, DRDO has developed a hybrid split-antenna configuration. The aircraft combines a large dorsal AESA radar with an additional nose-mounted radar array, providing approximately 300 degrees of active surveillance coverage.
The forward radar is intended to eliminate blind zones directly ahead of the aircraft while improving detection performance during forward-sector operations. Combined with extensive indigenous Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) and Communications Intelligence (COMINT) systems, the architecture is optimised for India’s operational environment.
Although the Netra Mk2 does not provide full 360-degree radar coverage like the E-7, its design reflects DRDO’s emphasis on balancing capability, complexity and indigenous development within programme constraints.
Mission Systems and Network Integration
Mission-system philosophy also differs considerably. The E-7 Wedgetail typically accommodates around 10 mission operator consoles, supporting a crew complement of up to 21 personnel. It integrates seamlessly into NATO command-and-control networks using systems such as Link 16, enabling direct coordination with fifth-generation aircraft including the F-35 Lightning II.
The aircraft functions as a highly capable airborne battle management platform, coordinating fighter aircraft, naval assets and ground forces across large operational theatres.
The Netra Mk2, meanwhile, has been designed specifically for the Indian Air Force’s operational doctrine.
Its reconfigurable operator workstations are expected to integrate closely with India’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS), enabling seamless networking with indigenous and imported air defence assets. The mission system has been tailored to address India’s unique threat environment, including low-observable drones, cruise missiles and potential stealth aircraft operating across both the western and northern fronts.
Industrial Ecosystem
The programmes also differ in their industrial foundations. The E-7 Wedgetail benefits from Boeing’s mature global aerospace supply chain and decades of support experience backed by major Western defence contractors.
By contrast, the Netra Mk2 represents one of India’s most ambitious indigenous aerospace collaborations. Aircraft conversion is being undertaken by AIESL, while Adani Defence Systems & Technologies Limited serves as the Development-cum-Production Partner (DcPP) responsible for mission-system integration and long-term sustainment under a 30-year lifecycle support agreement. This model is intended to ensure that critical maintenance, upgrades and logistics remain within India’s domestic industrial ecosystem.
A Different Benchmark
Although comparisons with the E-7 Wedgetail are inevitable, the Netra Mk2 is not intended to be a direct replica of the Western platform. Instead, it reflects India’s strategy of developing an indigenous AEW&C capability tailored to its own operational requirements while maximising domestic industrial participation.
The E-7 remains the world’s most mature and combat-proven narrow-body AEW&C aircraft, offering proven 360-degree radar coverage, established global logistics and extensive operational experience. The Netra Mk2, meanwhile, seeks to leverage the larger Airbus A321 platform, indigenous AESA radar technology, integrated ELINT/COMINT capabilities and deep integration with India’s IACCS network to deliver a sovereign airborne surveillance capability.

evening.title: IAF Undertaking 60 Defence Programmes with DRDO and Private Sector, ₹21,000 Crore Opportunities Identified
evening.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) has significantly expanded its indigenous capability development efforts, with more than 60 programmes currently being undertaken in collaboration with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and the Indian private sector. The initiative reflects the service’s growing emphasis on self-reliance and the development of advanced homegrown technologies to meet future operational requirements.
Speaking at a CNBC-TV18 event, Air Vice Marshal Tejpal Singh AVSM, VM, Assistant Chief of Air Staff (Plans), revealed that the IAF is currently working on at least 60 programmes involving DRDO and private industry. He also highlighted that these initiatives collectively represent business opportunities exceeding ₹21,000 crore, with the majority expected to be executed by private-sector companies.
The announcement underscores a fundamental shift in India’s defence procurement strategy. Rather than relying predominantly on imports or public sector undertakings, the IAF is increasingly partnering with private enterprises to accelerate the development of indigenous systems while strengthening the domestic defence industrial ecosystem.
Although specific details of the programmes were not disclosed, the IAF’s ongoing modernisation plans encompass a broad range of technologies. These include advanced avionics, electronic warfare systems, communication equipment, sensors, radars, mission computers, artificial intelligence-enabled applications, unmanned aerial systems, precision-guided munitions, airborne networking solutions and maintenance technologies. Many of these projects are being pursued under the broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative aimed at reducing India’s dependence on foreign defence suppliers.
The ₹21,000 crore opportunity represents a substantial boost for India’s private defence industry. Over the past decade, private companies have steadily expanded their role from manufacturing components to developing complete defence systems. Firms ranging from established defence manufacturers to startups are now participating in programmes involving aerospace, propulsion, electronics, autonomous systems and next-generation military technologies.
The Indian Air Force has emerged as one of the strongest advocates of indigenous capability development, supporting programmes such as the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft, Astra beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, Uttam Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar, indigenous electronic warfare suites and advanced weapon integration projects. The service has also been working closely with DRDO and industry on technologies that will support future platforms, including the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) and unmanned combat aerial systems.
The collaboration between the IAF, DRDO and private industry is expected to shorten development timelines by leveraging the innovation and manufacturing capabilities available across India’s growing defence ecosystem. The Defence Ministry has increasingly encouraged such partnerships through initiatives like the Technology Development Fund (TDF), Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and various Make-I and Make-II programmes, enabling private firms to contribute directly to the development of advanced military capabilities.
Beyond strengthening operational readiness, these programmes are expected to create long-term opportunities for Indian industry in both domestic procurement and defence exports. As indigenous technologies mature and enter service with the armed forces, they can potentially be offered to friendly foreign nations, further supporting India’s ambition of becoming a major global defence manufacturing hub.

evening.title: India Prepares Comprehensive Flight Trials for Indigenously Developed Missile and Precision Weapon Systems
evening.text:
The Indian defense establishment is gearing up for a major series of trials focusing on advanced, homegrown weapon platforms designed to significantly curtail reliance on imported military hardware. According to defense reports, upcoming evaluations will feature critical milestones for multiple domestically engineered munitions, encompassing advanced beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles, anti-radiation systems, and precision-guided standoff glide bombs.
At the forefront of these evaluations are the Astra series of air-to-air missiles. The operational roadmap includes live-firing trials for the Astra-2 missile—boasting a 160-kilometer range—following successful carriage and dummy-drop checks from a frontline Sukhoi-30MKI fighter. Concurrently, the 100-kilometer range Astra-1 is slated for evaluation utilizing an entirely indigenous seeker developed to replace legacy Russian AGAT guidance units. The Indian Air Force has already contracted an initial batch of 250 Astra-1 units to equip its Su-30MKI fleet, with integration initiatives also underway for Tejas and MiG-29 platforms. Furthermore, development on the ramjet-powered Astra-3 aims to push operational striking distances up to 350 kilometers.
Complementing the air-to-air inventory, the schedule highlights trials for the Rudram-1 New Generation Anti-Radiation Missile, engineered with a 150-kilometer range to systematically neutralize hostile radar, communication, and electronic surveillance assets. Defense research agencies are also advancing longer-range iterations including the Rudram-2 and Rudram-3 variants to fortify suppression of enemy air defense capabilities. To round out the tactical strike portfolio, smart anti-airfield weapons and heavy-caliber glide bomb inventories designed for localized runway and hardened bunker denial are moving through active deployment pipelines.

evening.title: Mount Toba eruption doesn't seem like it could nearly kill our species
evening.text:
Mount Toba was the biggest volcanic eruption in the last 2.6 million years, and some have suggested it nearly wiped out humanity. Around 74,000 years ago, a caldera on what is now Sumatra emptied thousands of cubic kilometers of magma in about two weeks, roughly a thousand times more than Mount Pinatubo spewed out in 1991. “People thought it might have caused massive cooling of the planet, and hence threatened the survival of our ancestors,” says Jinheum Park, a geoscientist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany.

Park and his colleagues went looking for the records of that catastrophe in the mud taken from the bottom of a small crater lake on the Kenya-Tanzania border. They found instead that the effects of the Mount Toba eruption lasted under two years and amounted to perhaps half a degree of cooling.

Muddy calendars

Volcanic eruptions inject sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it becomes a haze of tiny droplets that reflect sunlight back into space. Bigger eruptions eject more sulfur dioxide and, in principle, cause more cooling. But this trend stops working when the eruption exceeds a certain magnitude. “Bigger sulfate aerosols settle quickly, because they are heavier,” Park explains. This quick settling makes them less effective in scattering incoming solar radiation.
